title: Rethinking Graph Backdoor Attacks: A Distribution-Preserving Perspective

problem.claim: Graph Neural Networks are vulnerable to backdoor attacks in which poisoned training graphs cause triggered test nodes to be classified as a target class.

gap.claim: Existing graph backdoor triggers tend to be out-of-distribution, making them detectable and prunable with common outlier-detection methods.

contributions.claim: An OOD detector combined with adversarial learning generates trigger attributes within the data distribution.
Novel modules enhance memorization of in-distribution triggers by a victim model trained on a poisoned graph.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper studies the novel problem of unnoticeable graph backdoor attacks using in-distribution triggers and introduces novel modules for trigger memorization.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets report that the proposed method generates in-distribution triggers that bypass various defense strategies while maintaining a high attack success rate.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNNs perform well across various tasks.
GNNs are vulnerable to graph backdoor attacks that poison training graphs and redirect triggered test nodes to a target class.
Existing triggers are often out-of-distribution and can be detected and pruned.
The paper proposes in-distribution triggers generated through OOD detection, adversarial learning, and enhanced trigger memorization.
Experiments on real-world datasets report effective trigger generation, defense bypass, and high attack success.

source_observation.claim: Out-of-distribution triggers differ substantially from clean data and are vulnerable to outlier detection.

interpretation.claim: Backdoor stealth may require preserving the data distribution, not only increasing attack effectiveness.

application.claim: When designing graph backdoor attacks, evaluate whether trigger attributes remain in-distribution and withstand detection-based defenses.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify how the approach behaves across datasets, trigger settings, or defenses beyond the reported experiments.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide dataset names, baseline methods, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not describe the OOD detector, adversarial-learning objective, or memorization modules in technical detail.
The abstract does not specify which defense strategies were evaluated or how attack success was measured.
